definition: Implicit knowledge is knowledge that develops through repeated exposure without formal instruction or conscious awareness. In this source, it refers to non-speakers becoming familiar with the forms and patterns of a language, and in some cases showing limited meaning knowledge as well.

reasons: The definition adds unsupported generalities not stated in the packet, including that the knowledge develops through repeated exposure, without formal instruction, and without conscious awareness.

The packet supports familiarity with Māori word-forms and phonotactic/morphological knowledge from exposure, but it does not define implicit knowledge itself as a general learning concept in the way the definition states.

The claim about ‘limited meaning knowledge’ is only partially supported; the packet says some word meanings were identified relatively well and that different levels of semantic knowledge exist, but it does not support the broader definitional phrasing as written.

The definition claims implicit knowledge “develops … without formal instruction or conscious awareness,” but the provided packet text does not state or support that characterization (it only describes participants being “regularly exposed” to Māori).

The rest of the definition is only partially supported: the packet supports that non-Māori-speaking people exposed to Māori develop knowledge of word forms/patterns (proto-lexicon; phonotactic/morphological knowledge) and that the “without semantics” claim may be oversimplified, implying some semantic-related differences across words; however, the unsupported “without formal instruction or conscious awareness” clause prevents a full pass.
